newsitem.title: USA: NYC Council wants tech jobs, mayor defends record.
newsitem.headline: NYC Council wants tech jobs, mayor defends record.

text.p: The New York City Council, predicting bigger revenues than Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, wants some of the funds spent on parks, schools and recycling, as targeted tax breaks to create high-techology jobs.

But Giuliani defended his Administration's success in turning around the city's economy with broad tax relief, like lowering the commercial rent tax, which he told reporters was the biggest such reduction in New York City's history. "Our program for job growth is to continue those general incentives for business that have been so successful."
Saying his policies had created 120,000 private sector jobs, Giuliani added the city's economy lost over 300,000 jobs in the early 1990s, under the previous administration.

Looking at the fat profits earned by Wall Street banks and brokers, the City Council, whose estimates for revenues recently have been accurate, projected that the city will get $146 million more than the mayor expects in tax revenues for fiscal 1997, which ends on June 30, and an extra $356 million in revenues for the next year.

Noting the city, which has had to close $14 billion of budget gaps since 1990, when it was hit by a sharp, local, recession, Council Speaker, Peter Vallone, a Democrat, outlined a program he said would use the city's financial turnaround to safeguard its future.

He also faulted the mayor for failing to come up with a strategy to grow the city's economy. "Mayor Giuliani's budget is missing something--a vision for job growth," Vallone said, in prepared remarks. The City Council recommended targeted tax cuts to help "emerging industries," in high-technolgy areas, from medicine to software, as well as a plan to give small business owners a reason to both live and work in the city.
The Republican mayor dismissed the Council's criticism as driven by party politics. "I think there's a little bit of partisanship in some of the language of the press release."
The biggest part of the tax cuts proposed by the City Council would be an unincorporated business tax credit on the personal income tax break that would cost $76 million in fiscal 1998.

A $45 million plan would give qualified companies a five-year tax moratorium if they kept at least 75 percent of their payroll in the city for the next 10 years and employeed less than 100 workers during an initial period. These industries have around 50,000 workers, a workforce the Council hopes its plan would help double over the next several years.

The City Council also laid out some other different spending priorities, with Enoch Williams, who chairs the health committee, signalling it would fight some of the mayor's plans. Saying healthcare had to be protected, he noted as an example that while 43 clinics were transferred last year to the Health and Hospitals Corp, which got funding for them from the Department of Health, such revenues were not provided in the new budget.

Herber Berman, who chairs the Council's finance committee, said the city should use some of the extra dollars for museums and other cultural institutions, whose budgets Giuliani has cut, and which also create jobs. The Council would give such entities $28 million more, with libraries getting $25 million.
Parks would have $17 million more to spend, while youth programs would gain $20 million. And recycling, another area the mayor has cut, would get $19 million.

The Council also offered a plan to stabilize the city's finances, which are vulnerable not only to a recession but to a drop in financial markets as Wall Street firms and their high-income employees account for so much of its tax base.

About 40 percent of the extra revenues, or $225 million, would be deposited in a Rainy Day Fund, which could be tapped if the economy turned sour, under the Council's plan. New York State, along with a number of other states, has such a fund, and Vallone said he did not expect problems getting Albany's approval, which would be needed.
